drills.q: A churn model reports 98% AUC in cross-validation, far above any comparable benchmark. What's your first hypothesis and how do you check it?
drills.a: Suspect leakage before a breakthrough -- genuine improvements on well-studied problems come in modest increments, so an implausible jump is more likely an information shortcut. Check feature importances for one implausibly dominant feature, trace its real-world data-generation timing against the prediction point, and try removing it to see if performance collapses toward the expected range.

drills.q: A colleague computes a rolling 30-day feature with df.groupby('user_id').rolling(30).mean() directly on sorted data. What's the bug?
drills.a: Pandas' rolling window includes the current row by default -- if the intent is 'average of the prior 30 days, not including today,' this leaks the row's own value into its own feature. Fix by shifting the window by 1 row (or by the actual reporting lag) before rolling.

drills.q: A time-series forecasting model backtests excellently but performs poorly the week after deployment. Diagnose.
drills.a: Random k-fold CV was likely used instead of time-respecting CV, giving the model an implicit look-ahead advantage (training on 'future' relative to some validation rows) that production never has. Switch to TimeSeriesSplit or rolling-window backtesting and expect the honest validation number to be meaningfully lower.

drills.q: A churn model trained on multiple snapshots per user performs far worse on brand-new users than validation predicted. What CV mistake caused this and what's the fix?
drills.a: Plain k-fold let some of a user's rows land in training and others in validation, letting the model memorize per-user idiosyncrasies rather than genuinely generalize. Fix: GroupKFold keyed on user ID, so each user's entire row set goes to exactly one fold -- expect validation metrics to drop toward a more honest new-user estimate.

drills.q: Your production system continuously retrains to predict the NEXT snapshot for already-known users, not genuinely new users. Is GroupKFold still the right CV choice?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- if the true production task is within-group prediction (same known users, next snapshot) rather than cross-group generalization, GroupKFold's stricter unseen-entity estimate could understate real achievable performance. CV strategy must match the actual deployment scenario, not be applied as an unconditional rule.

drills.q: You're predicting hospital readmission from multi-year patient visit records. Design the CV strategy and name the single most important leakage check.
drills.a: Combine group and time: assign whole patients to folds (no patient split across train/val) while also respecting temporal order if the production system predicts forward for new visits. Most important check: audit every feature for whether it could only be known AFTER the readmission outcome is determined (e.g., a discharge summary finalized only once the outcome is known) -- medical records are a well-documented high-risk domain for this kind of leakage.

drills.q: After fixing a group-leakage bug, validation AUC drops 15 points from what the previous team reported. How do you communicate this to an excited stakeholder?
drills.a: Present both numbers with a clear explanation of what each measures: the old ungrouped number reflects a mix of genuine pattern learning and per-patient/user memorization that won't generalize to new entities; the new grouped number is the honest estimate of new-entity generalization, which is what production will actually face. The lower number should drive the go/no-go decision, and explaining the mechanism (not just asserting correctness) is what earns trust.

drills.q: A rolling aggregate feature is correctly computed using only strictly-prior data in the training pipeline. Is the feature now guaranteed leakage-free in production?
drills.a: Not necessarily -- if training used a batch process with more complete/less-noisy historical data than what's actually available in the live serving path (e.g. a nightly job without the production data-completeness lag), there's a training/serving skew that behaves like leakage: validation performance won't replicate in production even though temporal leakage in the strict sense was avoided.
